data.title: Scabies — viva
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Scabies** (Infestations)_

**Q1. Define scabies and describe the mite.**
- Contagious infestation by Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis; oval, flattened mite ~0.4 mm (female), 4 pairs of legs, transmitted by prolonged skin-to-skin contact

**Q2. Life cycle?**
- Fertilised female burrows in stratum corneum (2–3 mm/day), lays 2–3 eggs/day for 4–6 weeks; eggs hatch in 3–4 days; larvae → nymphs → adults in 10–14 days; usually 10–15 mites per patient (millions in crusted scabies)

**Q3. Why is itching worse at night and delayed in first infestation?**
- Type IV hypersensitivity to mite and its products develops in 3–6 weeks in first infestation (1–3 days in re-infestation); warmth at night increases mite activity and itch perception

**Q4. Clinical features and sites?**
- Nocturnal pruritus, family members affected, burrows (pathognomonic — grey serpiginous lines), papules, vesicles, nodules (male genitalia, axillae)
- Sites: finger webs, flexor wrists, elbows, axillary folds, areola, umbilicus, buttocks, genitalia (circle of Hebra); face and scalp spared in adults but involved in infants (also palms/soles)

**Q5. Types of scabies?**
- Classic, nodular, crusted (Norwegian — hyperkeratotic, thousands of mites, in immunocompromised/neurological/elderly; highly contagious), bullous (mimics pemphigoid), scabies incognito (steroid-treated), animal scabies (no burrows, exposed sites, self-limiting)

**Q6. Diagnosis?**
- Clinical (IACS 2020 criteria), burrow ink test, skin scraping with mineral oil/KOH (mite, eggs, scybala — faecal pellets), dermoscopy 'delta wing jet with contrail' sign, adhesive tape test, biopsy

**Q7. Differential diagnosis?**
- Infants: atopic dermatitis, infantile acropustulosis, papular urticaria
- Adults: insect bites, dermatitis herpetiformis, prurigo, contact dermatitis, HIV pruritus; elderly: asteatotic eczema, bullous pemphigoid

**Q8. Treatment?**
- Permethrin 5% cream neck down (whole body in infants/elderly) for 8–14 h, repeat after 7 days — first line (safe from 2 months, in pregnancy)
- Oral ivermectin 200 µg/kg repeated after 7–14 days (not <15 kg/pregnancy)
- Alternatives: benzyl benzoate 25%, precipitated sulphur 5–10% (infants, pregnancy), crotamiton
- Crusted: oral ivermectin on days 1, 2, 8, 9, 15 (± 22, 29) with topical permethrin and keratolytics
- Treat all close contacts simultaneously; launder clothes/bedding; antihistamines; post-scabetic itch lasts 2–4 weeks

**Q9. Complications?**
- Secondary impetigo, cellulitis, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (and possibly rheumatic heart disease in endemic communities), eczematisation, nodular scabies, lymphangitis

## Quick spotter facts
- Papules and burrows in finger webs with nocturnal itch in family members — scabies

_Sources: DYP Survival Guide for PG Dermatology Exam (Scabies); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e ch.22; Wolverton 4e ch.12 and ch.44. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
